paragraphs: Agamemnon proposes that the Achaeans should sail home, and Odysseus rebukes him—Hera deceives Zeus—Hector is wounded.

Nestor sat drinking his wine, but the noise of battle did not escape him. He said to the son of Asclepius, “Noble Machaon, what does all this mean? The shouts of men fighting by our ships keep growing louder. Stay here and go on with your wine, while fair Hecamede heats a bath for you and washes the clotted blood off your body. I will go straight to the lookout post and find out what is happening.”

He took the shield of his son Thrasymedes from the tent, where it lay gleaming with bronze, since Thrasymedes had taken his father’s shield. He also picked up his redoubtable bronze-shod spear. As soon as he was outside he saw the disastrous rout of the Achaeans. Their wall was overthrown, and they were fleeing in confusion before the Trojans. Think of a heavy swell on the sea when the waves are dumb. They watch for the quarter from which the fierce winds may spring on them, but they stay where they are and roll neither this way nor that, until some particular wind sweeps down from heaven to decide for them. In the same way the old man was torn over whether to make for the crowd of Danaans or go in search of Agamemnon. In the end he thought it best to go to the son of Atreus. Meanwhile the armies kept fighting and killing one another, and the hard bronze rattled on their bodies as they thrust at each other with swords and spears.

The wounded kings met Nestor as they came up from their ships: the son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon son of Atreus. Their ships were drawn up some way from the fighting, on the shore itself, because they had been beached first, and the wall had been built behind the hindmost. The shore, wide as it was, had no room for all the ships, and the army was cramped for space. So the ships had been placed in rows, one behind another, and they filled the whole opening of the bay between the two points that formed it. The kings were leaning on their spears and coming out to look at the fight. They were very anxious, and when old Nestor met them they were filled with dismay. King Agamemnon said to him, “Nestor son of Neleus, honor to the Achaean name, why have you left the battle and come here? I fear that dread Hector’s words will come true. He boasted among the Trojans that he would not go back to Ilium until he had set our ships on fire and killed us. That is what he said, and now it is all coming true. Alas! Other Achaeans, like Achilles, are so angry with me that they refuse to fight at the sterns of our ships.”

Then Nestor, knight of Gerene, answered, “It is just as you say. It is all coming true at this moment, and even Zeus who thunders from on high cannot stop it. The wall has fallen, the wall we trusted as an impregnable bulwark for ourselves and our fleet. The Trojans are fighting stubbornly at the ships and never let up. Look where you may, you cannot tell from what quarter the rout of the Achaeans is coming. They are being killed in a confused mass, and the battle cry rises to heaven. Let us think, if thinking can help, what we had better do. But I do not advise going into battle ourselves, for a man cannot fight when he is wounded.”

And King Agamemnon answered, “Nestor, the Trojans are indeed fighting at the rear of our ships, and neither the wall nor the trench has done us any good. The Danaans toiled so hard over them, and thought they would be an impregnable bulwark for ourselves and our fleet. So I see it must be the will of Zeus that the Achaeans should perish here without glory, far from Argos. I knew when Zeus was willing to defend us, and I know now that he is raising the Trojans to equal honor with the gods, while he has bound us hand and foot. Now let us all do as I say. Let us bring down the ships that are on the beach and draw them into the water. We will make them fast to their mooring stones a little way out, against the fall of night, in case the Trojans will stop fighting even by night. Then we may draw down the rest of the fleet. There is nothing wrong with fleeing from ruin, even by night. It is better for a man to flee and be saved than to be caught and killed.”

Odysseus looked fiercely at him and said, “Son of Atreus, what are you talking about? Wretch, you should have commanded some other, baser army, and not be ruler over us. Zeus has given us a life of hard fighting from youth to old age, until every one of us perishes. Is this how you would leave the city of Troy, which we have suffered so much hardship to win? Be quiet, or some other Achaean may hear you say what no man who knows how to give good counsel should ever have let fall from his lips, and no king over so great a host as the Argives. I utterly despise your judgment for what you have been saying. Would you have us draw our ships down into the water while the battle is raging, and so play further into the hands of the conquering Trojans? It would be ruin. The Achaeans will not go on fighting when they see the ships being drawn into the water. They will stop attacking and keep turning their eyes toward the ships. So your counsel, sir captain, would be our destruction.”

Agamemnon answered, “Odysseus, your rebuke has stung me to the heart. But I am not ordering the Achaeans to draw their ships into the sea against their will. Someone, old or young, may be able to offer us better advice, and I will be glad to hear it.”

Then Diomedes said, “That man is close by. You need not look far, if you will listen to me and not resent my speaking, though I am younger than any of you. By lineage I am the son of a noble father, Tydeus, who lies buried at Thebes. Portheus had three noble sons. Two of them, Agrius and Melas, lived in Pleuron and rocky Calydon. The third was the knight Oeneus, my father’s father, and he was the most valiant of them all. Oeneus stayed in his own country, but my father, as Zeus and the other gods ordained, moved to Argos. He married into the family of Adrastus. His house had great abundance: he had large estates of rich grain-growing land, with much orchard ground as well, and he had many sheep. He also excelled all the Argives in the use of the spear. You must have heard for yourselves whether these things are true. So when I speak well, do not despise my words as though I were a coward or of ignoble birth. I say, then, that we must go to the fight, wounded though we are. When we get there, we can stay out of the battle and beyond the range of spears, so that we get no fresh wounds on top of the ones we already have. But we can spur on the others, who have been indulging their ill temper and holding back from the battle until now.”
So he spoke. They did as he said and set out, with King Agamemnon in the lead.

Meanwhile Poseidon had been keeping a sharp lookout. He came up to them looking like an old man, took Agamemnon’s right hand in his own, and said, “Son of Atreus, I think Achilles is glad now, seeing the Achaeans routed and slain, for he has no remorse at all. May he come to a bad end, and may heaven confound him. As for you, the blessed gods are not yet so bitterly angry with you. The princes and counselors of the Trojans will again raise the dust on the plain, and you will see them fleeing from the ships and tents toward their city.”

With this he gave a mighty battle cry and rushed out to the plain. His voice came from a deep chest, and it was like the voice of nine or ten thousand men shouting in the thick of a fight. It gave the Achaeans fresh courage to wage war and fight without ceasing.

Hera of the golden throne stood on a peak of Olympus and looked down. Her heart was gladdened to see him who was both her brother and her brother-in-law hurrying back and forth amid the fighting. Then she turned her eyes to Zeus, sitting on the topmost crests of many-fountained Ida, and she loathed him. She set herself to think how she could hoodwink him. In the end she decided it was best to go to Ida dressed in rich attire, in the hope that Zeus would become enamored of her and want to embrace her. While he was occupied with that, a sweet and careless sleep might be made to steal over his eyes and senses.

She went, then, to the room her son Hephaestus had made for her. He had cunningly fastened its doors with a secret key, so that no other god could open them. She went in and shut the doors behind her. With ambrosia she cleaned all the dirt from her fair body, and then she anointed herself with olive oil, ambrosial, very soft, and scented specially for her. If it was so much as shaken in the bronze-floored house of Zeus, its scent filled the universe of heaven and earth. With this she anointed her delicate skin. Then she braided the fair ambrosial locks that flowed in a stream of golden tresses from her immortal head. She put on the wondrous robe that Athena had made for her with supreme skill and embroidered with many designs. She fastened it over her bosom with golden clasps, and belted herself with a girdle that had a hundred tassels. Then she put her earrings, three brilliant pendants that glistened most beautifully, through the pierced lobes of her ears, and threw a lovely new veil over her head. She bound her sandals on her feet. When she had dressed herself perfectly to her satisfaction, she left her room and called Aphrodite aside to speak to her. “My dear child,” she said, “will you do what I am going to ask of you, or will you refuse me because you are angry that I am on the Danaan side while you are on the Trojan?”

Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, answered, “Hera, august queen of goddesses and daughter of mighty Cronus, tell me what you want. I will do it for you right away, if I am able and if it can be done at all.”

Then Hera told her a lying tale. “I want you to give me some of those fascinating charms, whose spells bring all things, mortal and immortal, to your feet. I am going to the world’s end to visit Oceanus (from whom all we gods are descended) and mother Tethys. They received me in their house, took care of me, and brought me up, after taking me over from Rhaea when Zeus imprisoned great Cronus in the depths under earth and sea. I must go and see them to make peace between them. They have been quarreling, and are so angry that they have not slept with one another for a long while. If I can bring them around and restore them to one another’s embraces, they will be grateful to me and love me forever afterward.”
Laughter-loving Aphrodite replied, “I cannot and must not refuse you, since you sleep in the arms of Zeus, who is our king.”

As she spoke she unfastened from her bosom the curiously embroidered girdle in which all her charms had been wrought: love, desire, and that sweet flattery which steals the judgment even of the most prudent. She gave the girdle to Hera and said, “Take this girdle, which holds all my charms, and lay it in your bosom. If you wear it, I promise you that your errand, whatever it may be, will not fail.”
Hera smiled at these words, and still smiling she tucked the girdle into her bosom.

Aphrodite went back into the house of Zeus, and Hera darted down from the summits of Olympus. She crossed Pieria and fair Emathia and kept going until she reached the snowy mountains of the Thracian horsemen. She sped over their highest peaks without once touching the ground. At Athos she left the land and went on over the waves of the sea to Lemnos, the city of noble Thoas. There she met Sleep, own brother to Death. She caught his hand and said, “Sleep, you who rule over mortals and immortals alike, if you ever did me a service in the past, do one for me now, and I will be grateful to you ever after. Close the keen eyes of Zeus in slumber for me while I hold him clasped in my embrace. In return I will give you a beautiful golden seat that can never fall to pieces. My clubfooted son Hephaestus shall make it, with a footstool for you to rest your fair feet on when you are at table.”

Then Sleep answered, “Hera, great queen of goddesses, daughter of mighty Cronus, I would lull any other god to sleep without hesitation, even the waters of Oceanus, from whom all of them are descended. But I dare not go near Zeus, or send him to sleep unless he tells me to. I have already had one lesson from doing what you asked. It was the day when the mighty son of Zeus, Heracles, set sail from Ilium after sacking the city of the Trojans. At your bidding I poured my sweet self over the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus and laid him to rest. Meanwhile you hatched a plot against Heracles and set the blasts of the angry winds beating on the sea, until you carried him to the goodly city of Cos, away from all his friends. When Zeus woke he was furious, and began hurling the gods about all over the house. He was looking for me most of all, and would have flung me down through space into the sea, where I should never have been heard of again, if Night, who cows both men and gods, had not protected me. I fled to her, and Zeus left off looking for me, angry as he was, for he did not dare do anything to displease Night. And now you are asking me again to do something I cannot venture.”
